properties.title: Colorado River — 40M people, no post-2026 rules
properties.control_mismatch: The seven basin states could not reach agreement, so the decision passed to the Bureau of Reclamation. The resulting framework binds the Lower Basin to cuts it had already offered while leaving the Upper Basin without mandatory reductions — the asymmetry the compact created, now confirmed by federal decision rather than negotiated away.
properties.current_status: The states missed their deadline and Reclamation published a Final Environmental Impact Statement in the Federal Register on 31 July 2026, setting operations for Lake Powell, Lake Mead and associated infrastructure after the 2007 guidelines expire. For 2027-2028 it adopts the reductions the Lower Basin had proposed for itself; after 2028 it revises guidelines at two-year intervals through 2036. It imposes no mandatory reductions on the Upper Basin. Each state was required to file a detailed conservation plan by August 2026.
properties.who_depends: Las Vegas (90% from Colorado River), Phoenix/Tucson (Central Arizona Project), Southern California (Metropolitan Water District), Mexico (1.5M acre-feet/year allocation).
properties.who_controls: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation and the Secretary of the Interior, following the states' failure to agree. Upper Basin states (Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming) and Lower Basin states (Arizona, California, Nevada) retain compact entitlements but no longer control the operating rules.
properties.one_line: Seven states and 40M people depend on a river allocated during a wet period that overstated its flow. The states could not agree on successor rules, so in July 2026 the federal government wrote them instead — and the cuts fall on the Lower Basin.

sources.note: Post-2026 Colorado River Reservoir Operations Final EIS; Federal Register notice 31 July 2026
Analysis: Lower Basin reductions 2027-28, adaptive to 2036, no mandatory Upper Basin cuts

properties.title: Great Lakes Compact — anti-diversion rules with built-in exemptions
properties.governance: Great Lakes Compact Council (8 states + federal)
properties.control_mismatch: The Compact governs withdrawals by the basin states, but the barrier that protects the basin from invasive species is a federal construction project — so a stop-work order in Washington suspends a defence the states co-funded and cannot restart themselves.
properties.current_status: Waukesha has drawn Lake Michigan water since 9 October 2023 — the first diversion outside the basin approved under the Compact — capped at 8.2 million gallons a day, with return flow to the Root River and annual reporting. The Foxconn diversion was upheld by Wisconsin courts. The Brandon Road invasive-carp barrier, the physical defence of the basin, is now stopped: the Army Corps issued a stop-work order in late July 2026 and placed the $1.15B project under administrative review, after an earlier review from December 2025 to April 2026. Construction began in 2024 with completion expected in 2030. Illinois' governor has asked the administration to reverse it.
properties.who_depends: 34M people across 8 states and 2 Canadian provinces. Chicago metro area. Regional agriculture and industry. Municipal water systems throughout the basin.
properties.who_controls: 8-state Compact Council (ratified 2008). Individual state DNRs hold permit authority. Illinois self-regulates under pre-Compact exemption. Federal courts enforce the Compact but exceptions erode it.
properties.one_line: The Compact exists to prevent Great Lakes diversions. Illinois has a pre-Compact exemption. Waukesha got an exception. Foxconn got an exception. The anti-diversion framework keeps approving diversions.

sources.note: Stop-work order on Brandon Road; project under administrative review
Brandon Road Interbasin Project: $1.15B, construction from 2024, completion 2030
Waukesha diversion terms: 8.2 MGD, Root River return, annual reporting

properties.title: Ogallala Aquifer — 8 states mining groundwater with no interstate governance
properties.governance: Fragmented: local/state districts only. No interstate framework.
properties.control_mismatch: 8 states sit atop the same aquifer. No interstate compact, no basin-wide authority, no coordinated depletion limits. Each state manages (or doesn't) through local groundwater districts. Kansas has lost 44 feet of water depth. Recharge is 0.5-1 inch/year; withdrawal is 6+ feet/year in intensive zones. Federal crop subsidies incentivize water-intensive agriculture regardless of depletion.
properties.current_status: Depletion continues: the southwest Kansas management area fell 1.52 feet between January 2024 and January 2025, a steeper drop than the 1.43 feet the year before. Governance has changed, though. Under a Kansas law all five groundwater management districts had to file an action plan by 1 July 2026 or the state would impose one — the first hard deadline in the aquifer's history. Where local limits exist they work: farmers in the Sheridan LEMA self-imposed 20-30% cuts and met them without significant yield loss. There is still no binding interstate framework across the eight states.
properties.who_depends: Texas panhandle, Kansas, and Nebraska agriculture (the breadbasket). Municipal water for Lubbock, Amarillo, and smaller communities. 2.3M people directly; food system implications are national.
properties.who_controls: Whoever has a well. Texas Water Development Board + local districts. Kansas GMDs. Nebraska NRDs. No basin-wide authority exists. Control is atomized — essentially privatized extraction with no collective limits.
properties.one_line: Eight states drawing from the same aquifer with no interstate agreement. Recharge: 1 inch/year. Withdrawal: 6 feet/year. Governance: whoever has a well.

sources.note: Kansas 1 July 2026 district plan deadline; Sheridan LEMA 20-30% cuts

properties.title: Mississippi River — critical infrastructure dependent on seasonal flow with no long-term plan
properties.governance: Army Corps of Engineers (reactive emergency management)
properties.control_mismatch: Barge shipping, Memphis drinking water, New Orleans water supply, and power generation all depend on seasonal river flow. Army Corps can release upstream water but only reactively. No basin-wide low-water management plan exists. When the river dropped to -10.79 feet at Memphis (October 2022), 2,253 barges and 144 vessels queued. Shipping rates jumped from $11/ton to $71/ton.
properties.current_status: Not re-verified in the August 2026 refresh — No 2026 update located; searches returned only the 2022-23 low-water events. As recorded: 2022 drought is precedent for climate-driven low-water events. Corps has no long-term low-water strategy. Saltwater intrusion threatened New Orleans drinking water in 2023 (Gulf saltwater moves upstream when flow drops). Dependency is structural; management is reactive.
properties.who_depends: Barge shipping industry (grain, coal, oil). Memphis (largest artesian well system in North America). New Orleans (freshwater intake vulnerable to saltwater intrusion). Regional agriculture and power generation.
properties.who_controls: Army Corps of Engineers (dams, locks, emergency releases). National Weather Service (monitoring). No formal water allocation authority. Barge operators coordinate informally. Management is emergency-driven, not planned.
properties.one_line: The river dropped to its lowest level since 1954. Barges grounded, shipping rates jumped 6x, and the Corps had no plan because no plan exists.
properties.verification_note: No 2026 update located; searches returned only the 2022-23 low-water events.

properties.title: Apalachicola-Chattahoochee-Flint Basin — 40 years of litigation, no compact
properties.governance: Federal courts / Army Corps. No interstate compact.
properties.control_mismatch: Atlanta's 5.7M people depend on the Chattahoochee. Alabama and Florida receive diminishing downstream flows. Apalachicola Bay's oyster industry collapsed when freshwater flows dropped (salinity killed the oysters). 40+ years of litigation produced no binding interstate compact. 2023 settlement dismissed major lawsuits but established no permanent allocation framework.
properties.current_status: Not re-verified in the August 2026 refresh — No 2026 update located; the December 2023 settlement remains the last recorded development. As recorded: Settlement (Dec 2023) ended major litigation. Georgia committed to conservation measures but no binding compact. Future disputes likely as Atlanta continues growing. Army Corps operates dams and release schedules. Governance is federal court rulings and Corps negotiation, not interstate agreement.
properties.who_depends: Atlanta metro (5.7M, growing). Alabama agriculture and municipalities. Florida Apalachicola Bay ($5.8B historic fishing industry, now collapsed). Farm belt across all three states.
properties.who_controls: Army Corps (dam operations, release schedules). Federal courts (allocation disputes). Individual state water agencies (GA DNR, AL ADEM, FL DEP). No interstate compact — governance through litigation and Corps discretion.
properties.one_line: Atlanta keeps growing, Florida's oysters keep dying, and after 40 years of litigation there's still no interstate water compact.
properties.verification_note: No 2026 update located; the December 2023 settlement remains the last recorded development.

properties.title: Edwards Aquifer — 1.7M people vs an endangered fish, one aquifer
properties.control_mismatch: San Antonio's 1.7M people get 100% of drinking water from one sole-source aquifer. The fountain darter (endangered) lives only in spring-fed waters that dry up if the aquifer drops. Federal ESA lawsuit forced Texas to create the Edwards Aquifer Authority (1993) with pumping limits. Municipal demand vs species protection is a permanent structural tension.
properties.current_status: The San Antonio Pool has been under Critical Period Management continuously since March 2022. 2026 has been volatile: restrictions eased from Stage 4 to Stage 3 in the spring, to Stage 1 after heavy July rain, then back to Stage 2 on 6 August as levels fell again. Stage 2 requires permit holders authorised for more than 3 acre-feet a year — industrial and agricultural users — to cut authorised pumping by 30%. San Antonio has cut usage roughly 50% through conservation over the longer run, and the EAA retains enforcement authority.
properties.who_depends: San Antonio (1.7M people, 100% sole-source). Regional agriculture. Spring-fed ecosystems (Comal, San Marcos springs).
properties.who_controls: Edwards Aquifer Authority (pumping limits, spring flow protection). Created by ESA lawsuit — federal species protection effectively governs a city's water supply. Board includes municipal, agricultural, and environmental stakeholders.
properties.one_line: 1.7 million people get all their water from one aquifer. An endangered fish determines how much they can pump. The fish was there first.

sources.note: Stage 2 CPM declared 6 Aug 2026; 30% reduction for permits over 3 AF

properties.title: Klamath Basin — farmers vs fish, then the largest dam removal in US history
properties.governance: Bureau of Reclamation / ESA / FERC / Tribal co-management
properties.control_mismatch: Bureau of Reclamation built the irrigation project (200,000+ acres, 1,400 farms). Then ESA listed coho salmon (1997). Federal species protection overrode irrigation allocation. 2021 drought: irrigation shutoff, fish kills. Solution: 4 dams removed 2023-2024 (largest dam removal in US history), opening 425 miles of habitat. Farmers now face uncertain water availability under new managed flow regime.
properties.current_status: Dam removal completed October 2024, opening more than 400 miles of habitat. Salmon returned fast: a Chinook passed a former dam site within a week, and in October 2025 one was filmed ascending the fish ladder at Keno Dam in the upper basin — the first in over a century. The allocation fight is now between restored fish and irrigators rather than between dams and fish. For the 2026 season Reclamation allocated 221,000 acre-feet from Upper Klamath Lake, 63% of a normal year, plus 35,000 acre-feet each from Gerber and Clear Lake. Snowpack vanished from the upper basin early.
properties.who_depends: 1,400 farms (200,000+ acres). Endangered coho salmon. Tribal fisheries (Klamath tribes, treaty rights). Downstream commercial fisheries.
properties.who_controls: Bureau of Reclamation (irrigation, allocation). FERC (dam licensing — now removed). ESA (NOAA Fisheries, USFWS — species override). Klamath tribes (co-management, treaty rights). Federal authority overrides local when species are listed.
properties.one_line: The feds built the irrigation project, then listed the fish, then removed the dams. Farmers got the water, then lost it, then got uncertainty.

sources.note: 2026 allocation: 221,000 AF (63% of normal) plus Gerber and Clear Lake

properties.title: Flint & Detroit — water as governance lever in emergency management
properties.governance: State emergency manager system / Great Lakes Water Authority
properties.control_mismatch: Flint's contamination came from a state-appointed emergency manager overriding local government, and its remedy came from a federal settlement — neither decided locally. Detroit's affordability crisis persists because no permanent funding authority exists at any level: the city runs a programme it cannot fund, the regional authority sets the rates, and the federal programme is a bill, not a law.
properties.current_status: Flint: the final active lead service line was replaced on 31 July 2026, roughly 11,600 lines out of nearly 32,000 properties excavated in a ~$140M programme under a federal settlement, with a decade of compliance with state and federal lead standards. Detroit: unresolved. About 170,000 households have faced shutoffs since 2014. The Lifeline H2O affordability plan never secured permanent funding, enrolled 4,711 households, and closed to new applicants when its funding ran out. The Great Lakes Water Authority raised water rates 5.8% and sewer rates 4.26% in February 2026. A federal low-income water affordability programme has been reintroduced in Congress but does not exist.
properties.who_depends: Flint (100K). Detroit metro (680K city, 4M+ metro). Both on Great Lakes — abundant water.
properties.who_controls: Michigan state emergency manager system (appointed, unelected, overrides elected officials). Great Lakes Water Authority (regional). The control mismatch is governance, not hydrology — abundant water, managed to produce scarcity.
properties.one_line: Both cities sit on the Great Lakes. Flint finished replacing its lead pipes in July 2026, a decade after an unelected manager switched the water to save money. Detroit's problem was never lead — it is that people cannot pay, and that has not been fixed.

sources.note: Final active lead service line replaced 31 July 2026; ~11,600 of ~32,000 properties

sources.publisher: State of Michigan (Office of the Governor)

sources.note: Lifeline H2O at capacity, closed to new applicants; 4,711 enrolled
